match.reason: No point in the bank covers setting prices and positioning across countries; the closest ones, on global businesses and economic influences, are related but broader ideas taught at Year 11 depth.

draft.title: Global pricing and positioning
card: A business selling in many countries must set a price for each market. The same price everywhere is rarely the best choice.
Pricing
the price allows for costs such as shipping, tariffs and taxes, the prices of local rivals, exchange rates, and what local customers can afford.
Currency
if the Australian dollar rises against the buyer's currency, the product costs more for that buyer unless the seller cuts its Australian dollar price.
Positioning
the business chooses how customers see its product compared with local rivals, such as premium quality, low price or a trusted import.
draft.remember: Global prices and positioning are set market by market, using costs, rivals, currency and incomes.

a.q: An Australian skincare firm sells in a country where average incomes are much lower than in Australia. Which pricing step best fits the card?
opts: Set a price that local customers can afford
Charge the Australian price to protect its image
Ignore local rivals so the price stays simple
Set the price using only its Australian costs
a.why: Local incomes decide what customers can afford, so the price is set to suit that market. Charging the Australian price ignores incomes, which the card says a global price must allow for.
a.clue: Think about what local customers can afford.

b.q: Hana exports Australian-made backpacks to Japan. The Australian dollar rises against the yen, and she keeps her Australian dollar price the same. What is the likely effect on Japanese buyers?
opts: The backpacks cost more in yen for them
The backpacks cost less in yen for them
The price in yen stays the same for them
Local rivals must raise their yen prices
b.why: When the Australian dollar rises, each Australian dollar costs more yen. With an unchanged Australian dollar price, the yen price goes up. It would stay the same only if Hana cut her Australian dollar price.
b.clue: A stronger Australian dollar buys more yen, so it costs buyers more.

a.best: Set a price that local customers can afford

b.best: The backpacks cost more in yen for them

problems.detail: The clue 'Think about what local customers can afford' repeats the wording of the right option, so a student can pick it without knowing the idea.
The clue 'so it costs buyers more' states the answer outright, so the question no longer tests the idea.
Why (a) says the card says a global price 'must' allow for incomes. The card says the price 'allows for' what customers can afford, so the why overstates the card.

check.summary: The card and both questions are accurate, but both clues give the answer away and should be rewritten as hints. Why (a) also uses 'must' where the card only says the price 'allows for' incomes.

opts: Set a price that local customers can afford
Charge the Australian price to protect its image
Ignore local rivals so the price stays simple
